Hi, I’m Ilaria. I wrote these guides to share what I’ve learned about RVC while developing Ilaria RVC, training voice models and working with other tools. The explanations and recommendations reflect my experience and what I understand at the time of writing. I can misunderstand a setting, miss an exception or describe a step that changes in a later release.

The same instructions can give different results on another computer. For example, a button might move after an update, a feature may depend on your GPU or driver, and settings that work for one voice might sound worse on another. When you see a suggested value, treat it as a starting point. Try it on a short clip and compare the result before using it on a whole project. Before replacing files or updating a working installation, keep a copy you can come back to.

If something doesn’t match what you see, check the app name, version and exact error first. Then compare with the release notes or the instructions for your build. If you spot a mistake, let me know which page and step you followed, which version you used and what happened. That gives me enough information to test the issue and improve the guide.
For any problems, suggestions or updates, contact me on Discord.

Retrieval-based voice conversion (RVC) takes a vocal recording and synthesizes a version with the character of a trained voice. The recording supplies the performance, including the words, rhythm and much of the pitch contour. The model determines how that performance is rendered. For a spoken line, record the pronunciation and delivery you want to hear in the result. A pitch adjustment changes the register without translating or rewriting the line.
A pitch predictor estimates the fundamental frequency, or F0, in voiced sections. Pitch-guided models can use this contour during synthesis.
An embedder represents the sound of each short section of the input. Common RVC workflows use ContentVec or a HuBERT-based feature extractor.
Clipped peaks, room echo and other voices can contaminate later stages.
Compare retrieval on and off if the result sounds muffled or the source timbre is too prominent.

Generic HuBERT checkpoints are not recommended as the default encoder for voice conversion. Their speech prediction training does not explicitly remove speaker identity, so the features can carry source timbre into the output. For RVC, use the encoder expected by the model, such as ContentVec when the voice was trained with it.

What it does
What to listen for
When a compatible index is available, the converter can blend nearby features from the model's training data with the source features.
Pitch shift offsets the detected contour by semitones. Start at zero and change it if the performance is outside the target voice's comfortable register.
Pitch predictor changes how the contour is measured. Compare predictors on a passage that contains the problem, such as a sustained note or the transition from talking to a breath.

Index rate changes the balance between source and retrieved features. Zero disables the retrieval contribution in standard RVC workflows. A high setting can emphasize characteristics of the training data, including unwanted artifacts.

Sample rate describes how many audio samples represent a second. The source file rate, the model's synthesis rate and the exported file rate can differ. Resampling a file changes its representation without making an incompatible checkpoint loadable.
For app-specific conversion controls, see Voice conversion.

Confirm the model family and architecture. Use a runtime that explicitly supports the model. Classic RVC v1 and v2 use different feature dimensions, commonly 256 and 768 respectively in RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC). Some forks also support architectures that require their own runtime.

Check the embedder. The runtime should supply the feature representation the model was trained to expect. A model trained with a custom embedder can need that embedder at inference time. A similar file extension or a matching sample rate alone provides little evidence of support.

Use the inference export. A ready-to-use .pth and a training checkpoint can have the same extension. Select the file identified by the publisher as the inference model. A ZIP is a container for the files and is only directly importable where the app supports ZIP import.

Pair retrieval data with its checkpoint. An .index built for another voice or embedder can fail or degrade the result. Keep the model and its index together and check that the app selected the expected pair. If you only have a compatible model, use the no-retrieval workflow supported by your client.
Test a short file. Try a clean clip with default settings. A model that loads can still sound wrong if the runtime uses the wrong feature extractor or the input is far outside the voice's range.

Obtain model files from the original publisher or another source you trust. Loading a PyTorch checkpoint can involve deserializing Python objects. Keep the protections in your loader enabled and request a supported export if it refuses a file. PyTorch loading reference

l: Judge the result with a repeatable test
p: Keep a dry reference clip and use that same clip for every comparison. Include a quiet phrase, a sentence with sharp consonants and a sustained vowel. Keep playback levels similar so that loudness alone does not make one output seem better.
Render a baseline using the app's defaults.
Check word clarity first. If both the dry and converted clips are hard to understand, re-record the source.
For pitch wobble, compare two supported pitch predictors before changing retrieval.
For a timbre or texture problem, compare with retrieval disabled, then adjust the index rate if the matching index helps.
Save the working settings with the model name, release and input. When a later update changes the sound, those notes give you a starting point.

l: Choose a model for the job
p: Listen to demos that resemble your intended input. For speech, listen for consonants, quieter words and natural pauses. For singing, check sustained notes and the high and low ends of your range. If you plan to use it live, test speaking freely and changing volume. Check the documented engine and model version, known language limitations and terms of use. A model that sounds good in one language may sound uneven in another, even when the training dataset includes both.
Download from a source you trust and read the included notes. Model files can be unsafe when loaded by software that deserializes arbitrary objects.
Keep each voice and version in its own folder, with the exported .pth, its optional .index and any notes. Filenames alone are insufficient to match an index to a model.

In Ilaria RVC, open Other → Import Local Models. Choose the inference .pth or a supported ZIP, then add the matching .index if you have it. Other apps may ask you to refresh the model list after import.
Record about ten seconds of one voice in a quiet room, without music, heavy reverb or clipping.
Select the intended model, leave index retrieval off and start at zero pitch shift. Save the converted WAV as a reference.
If the register sounds strained, compare small pitch changes in semitones using the same input. Pitch shift changes the register, so judge it separately from voice identity.

Once pitch is set, try a small increase in retrieval with the matching index. Listen for clearer voice character, then check whether breaths or consonants become rough. Keep the setting that sounds best, including zero.

What to check
The app cannot load the model
Confirm the engine, version and file type. Extract the ZIP if the importer rejects it, then select the exported inference weights.
The result still sounds like the source
Compare with another known-good model using the same clip. Persistent source timbre can come from the model or its training embedder, including HuBERT variants. More retrieval may not resolve it.
Breaths or consonants sound metallic
Compare with retrieval off. If the problem persists across clean inputs and settings, it may be in the model and require retraining.

Try the same model with a file. If file conversion works, check the microphone, audio routing and buffer in the live app.

l: Keep a model ready to reuse
p: Save the working app version, model version, selected pitch and retrieval settings with a short reference clip. Test again after changing apps or updating the model. If you train your own voices, keep the export for inference and the files needed to resume training in separate folders.

A pitch extractor (also called an F0 extraction method) is the algorithm or neural network that tracks the fundamental frequency (pitch, melody, and intonation) of the input voice over time.
While an embedder reads what words and phonemes are being spoken or sung, the pitch extractor measures how high or low the voice goes at every fraction of a second.

Compatibility: Unlike embedders, pitch extractors do not lock you into one choice. Even if a model was trained using rmvpe for dataset preprocessing, you can use any available pitch extractor during inference and live voice changing without breaking compatibility.
Best overall (Training & Conversion): rmvpe or rmvpe_gpu (if you have an NVIDIA GPU).
Best for Live / Real-time Voice Changers: fcpe (fastest latency) or rmvpe (best quality if your GPU keeps up).
Avoid for general use: pm, dio, and harvest are legacy CPU methods that sound noticeably worse or run much slower than rmvpe and fcpe.

l: rmvpe vs rmvpe_gpu: what is the difference?
p: In apps like Ilaria RVC and RVC Mainline, you will often see both rmvpe and rmvpe_gpu:
rmvpe may run on CPU or follow the app's default device scheduling, which uses less VRAM but can bottleneck on long files or big datasets.
rmvpe_gpu explicitly runs the RMVPE model on your CUDA GPU, delivering identical pitch quality at much higher speed during dataset feature extraction and offline conversion.
If rmvpe_gpu triggers CUDA out of memory on a low-VRAM card (4 GB or less), switch back to rmvpe or fcpe.

l: Choosing the right method for your task
p: Preparing / Training a new model: Use rmvpe_gpu (if you have an NVIDIA GPU with 6+ GB VRAM) or rmvpe. Clean dataset F0 tracking prevents pitch glitches in the trained voice.
Converting songs or voiceovers offline: Start with rmvpe or rmvpe_gpu. Only test crepe-full or hybrid if a specific high singing note has an octave jump.
Live microphone / Discord: Start with fcpe for lowest delay, or rmvpe if your GPU handles your chunk size smoothly without crackling.

An embedder (also called a content encoder) is the neural network that reads your input audio and converts what is being said or sung into numerical content features before the RVC voice model reconstructs it in the target speaker's timbre.

l: What an embedder does and how it works
p: In an RVC pipeline, the audio is split into separate streams of information:
Content (what you say): extracted frame by frame by the embedder (phonemes, pronunciation, articulation, and timing).
Pitch / F0 (the melody): extracted separately by a pitch tracker (such as RMVPE or FCPE).
Speaker timbre (who is speaking): supplied by the trained RVC .pth voice model (and optionally reinforced by a matching .index file).
Because the RVC generator is trained to expect features from one specific embedder, two rules always apply:

Training and inference must match: if a voice model was trained with contentvec, you must convert audio with contentvec. Using a different embedder during inference (or live conversion) causes distorted pronunciation, metallic artifacts, or a completely broken voice.

Speaker-identity leakage: generic speech-recognition encoders (such as standard HuBERT models) were not trained to strip out the original speaker's identity. Using them can cause your own voice timbre to bleed into the converted output.

l: When you actually need to touch the embedder setting
p: Leave it on Auto or contentvec for almost every voice model and training run.

Only change it if you downloaded a pre-trained voice whose author explicitly states it was trained with a specific embedder (for example spin-v2 or japanese-hubert-base). Even then, only change it for inference on that specific model, not as your default for new training.
Do not switch embedders mid-training: changing the embedder requires re-extracting features (3_feature768) in a separate experiment.

A pretrained base model (also called a pretrain) is a pair of starting checkpoint files: a Generator (G_*.pth) and a Discriminator (D_*.pth), already trained on hundreds of hours of multi-speaker audio. When you train a new RVC voice, training does not start from scratch; instead, it fine-tunes this pretrained pair on your target speaker's dataset.

l: What pretrained models do and why they exist
p: Starting from a pretrained pair allows RVC to learn a new voice in minutes or hours instead of weeks:
The Generator (G) already knows how to turn content features and pitch into natural speech or singing.
The Discriminator (D) already knows how to judge whether generated audio sounds realistic or artificial.
Your training run adapts those existing weights to your target voice.
Every pretrained pair is locked to specific architectural parameters that must match your training setup exactly:
Sample rate (32 kHz, 40 kHz, 44.1 kHz, or 48 kHz)
Vocoder architecture (HiFi-GAN, RefineGAN, or MRF HiFi-GAN)
RVC version & pitch guidance (almost all community pretrains are RVC v2 with F0 pitch guidance)
Expected embedder (usually contentvec, though some variants require spin-v2)
If any of these settings do not match the pretrained pair, training will either crash immediately or produce heavily distorted audio.

First check
A voice is missing from Voice Model
Check the import log, then click Refresh. Select an inference .pth export. A G or D training checkpoint belongs to the experiment.
A file fails to decode

Conversion fails only with the index

l: Start here with the updated notebook

p: Open your editable copy on Kaggle and keep it private. The launch cell prints passwords. Keep its output out of screenshots, shared logs and published versions.

p: The Start → Access Setup section has two options. Leave Gradio + Cloudflare selected for a first test. Gradio opens Ilaria RVC, and Cloudflare opens FileBrowser. If you choose Horizon, enter the Horizon ID from your Horizon dashboard and approve the CLI token request when prompted. Horizon produces separate links for the same two services.

l: Tune training only after a short test
p: Setting
What to do for the first run
Training Precision
The notebook starts with FP16 when all visible GPUs are T4. Try FP32 for a comparison if needed. When resuming, match the existing checkpoint's configuration.
Batch Size

The UI value is per GPU for a fresh run with this notebook. One T4 at batch 8 and two T4s at batch 4 both give a global batch of 8 when those are the devices used by the run. Check the effective values in Training Log. Start smaller if memory is tight.
Workers and prefetch

Leave them at 2 each for the first run. The notebook suggests 4 workers and prefetch 8 when comparing with the older loader configuration. Change one factor at a time and compare the timing in train.log.
Fused AdamW
Leave it off at first. Test it in a new run if you want to compare performance. Keep the original batch configuration when resuming.
Two GPUs do not pool their VRAM into a single larger device. If a run runs out of memory, reduce the per-GPU batch and verify the effective settings in the log before retrying.

After conversion or after Stop and save confirms the checkpoint, set EXPORT = True and run Export results. Leave TRAINING_MODEL blank for regular model and audio exports, or enter the exact model name to include its resumable experiment files. Open FileBrowser or use the link displayed by the export cell and download Ilaria-RVC-results.zip. The archive is written in /kaggle/working/ilaria-shared. Confirm you can open it locally before closing the session.

When finished, set STOP = True and run Stop or restart. This shuts down the WebUI, FileBrowser and their tunnels. To reopen them in the same session, rerun section 4. To refresh the app code, save your work, stop the services, and rerun steps 1–4.

In the Ilaria RVC browser tab, open Other → Import local models. Upload the inference model file (.pth) and, optionally, its matching index file (.index). You can also upload a supported ZIP containing those files. Wait for the import to finish. Or open Other → Download models from Hugging Face, Google Drive or MEGA, paste a publicly downloadable link to a supported ZIP, .pth, or .index, and click Download and install model. If the model and its optional index are hosted separately, download them one at a time using the same panel.
Open Inference, refresh the voice list if needed, select the intended voice, and go to Single Inference.
Upload the short WAV. Start at Pitch 0 and Index Ratio 0. Leave the optional effects off and use the embedder expected by the model.
Click the conversion control once and wait for the output. Play the result, then download it from the player if available. Keep your input WAV so you can compare the same phrase later.

If you want to test retrieval, select the matching index and try a small increase from zero. If the output fails or the voice becomes harder to understand, return to the baseline and verify the model–index pairing.
If the voice never appears, first check the import log. A training checkpoint saved as a G or D file belongs to an experiment and needs an inference export before it can be selected here.

l: Prepare your dataset and plan a training run
Clean the audio with MVSEP only where needed
p: Keep an untouched copy of your recordings. If they already contain a single clean, dry voice, skip separation. Use material you have permission to upload to MVSEP and to train on. For confidential recordings, clean them locally.

Isolate the voice. Upload a short example and choose a vocal separation option. Download the vocal stem in WAV when available. Replay it against the original and listen through headphones for music, other voices, clipped syllables, and watery or metallic artifacts.

Remove backing vocals only if present. For songs with harmonies or a chorus underneath the target, use a lead-versus-backing separation option on the vocal stem. Keep the lead output. If the singers still overlap or the lead has holes, use a clean section or a different take.

Reduce reverb only where audible. If the voice has a wide stereo reverb tail, first test a stereo de-reverb option on a copy. For remaining room reflections, compare a room de-reverb pass. You can skip either stage. Listen for truncated consonants and breaths at each pass.

Remove echo only if it repeats the voice. An audible delayed repeat calls for a separate short test. Keep the original or replace that take if removal strips out words. Avoid stacking passes on otherwise clean audio.

Prepare the final clips. Trim unusable noise and long empty sections in an editor such as Audacity, while keeping useful breaths and natural phrasing. Export clean WAVs. Put the approved files together in a ZIP and keep a few clean clips outside it for evaluation.

Test the full cleanup chain on a few seconds before treating the entire dataset. A model can learn artifacts that are left in its training audio. Check several clips from different sessions before uploading.

l: Clean a dataset locally with Ultimate Vocal Remover (UVR)
p: UVR separates an audio file into tracks called stems. Use it when the target voice is mixed with music, sound effects or other vocals. If you already have a clean voice recording, keep the original. UVR processes audio on your computer after the required models are downloaded. Cloud runs the later RVC training job separately.

l: Install UVR and prepare a test clip
p: Download the installer or package for your operating system from UVR releases. Launch the desktop app after installing it.
Make a 15–30 second copy of an example that contains a clear line and a section where the music overlaps it. Keep the original safe.
Click Select Input and choose that test clip. Use Select Output to choose a new writable folder, such as uvr-test. Choose WAV for the output format.

Select a Process Method and a model that separates vocals from instrumental, for example a vocals model under MDX-Net. If the list is empty, open the settings Download Center, select the corresponding model family and download a suitable model. Return to the main window and select it.

Enable GPU Conversion only if your installed build recognizes a supported device. If that option causes an error, turn it off and test on the CPU. CPU processing can be slower, so start with a short clip.

Click Start Processing. When it finishes, find the vocals stem in the output folder. Some models also write an instrumental stem. Play the original and the vocals stem at similar volume. Check consonants, breaths, held notes, and sections where the accompaniment is loud. If you still hear instruments or the voice sounds watery or metallic, compare another model on the same test clip before processing the full dataset.
If you've selected the wrong stem, check the filenames or listen to each output. Keep the one that contains your target lead voice.

l: Clean the remaining problems one at a time
p: What remains
What to try in UVR
Backing vocals or harmonies
Feed the isolated vocal stem into a model intended for lead and backing separation, if your installation offers one. Keep the lead output and verify that the target vocal is complete.
Reverb tails between phrases
Try a model intended for de-reverb if available. Compare before and after on the same passage. Keep the original stem if de-reverb damages consonants or held notes.
Audible delayed repeats
Test an echo-removal model if available. If it removes words or distorts breaths, use another take or exclude the affected section.
Room hum, clipped peaks or other voices

Your dataset is the single biggest factor deciding how natural, clean, and expressive your RVC voice model will sound. Even the best training settings cannot fix noisy, reverberant, or distorted source recordings.
Golden rule: Quality always beats quantity. 10 minutes of dry, clean, varied single-speaker audio will train a much better voice model than 60 minutes of echoey, noisy, or repetitive clips.

l: 1. What makes a great RVC dataset

p: Minimum usable length: Around 5 to 10 minutes of pure speech or singing (excluding silence) can produce a working voice if the audio is very clean.
Recommended target: 15 to 30+ minutes of clean, varied audio gives the model enough phonetic coverage to handle different words, pitches, and emotions naturally.

Vocal variety matters: Include calm speech, energetic speech, different pitches, soft and loud phrases, and clear consonants (s, f, t, k). If you only train on monotone speech, the model will struggle when you sing or speak expressively.
One speaker only: Never leave overlapping voices, crowd noise, or backing harmonies in the dataset.
Dry room (minimal reverb): RVC learns room echo as part of the voice timbre. Close-mic studio recordings or dry voiceovers work best.
Lossless format: Prefer PCM .wav (or .flac) over low-bitrate .mp3 files whenever possible, so compression artifacts are not baked into the model.
No music or sound effects: Remove all background music, game audio, and SFX before preprocessing.
Separate vocals from music/SFX: If your source comes from songs, videos, or games, extract dry vocals first using UVR5 or MVSep.

Be careful with heavy denoising or dereverb: Only apply noise or reverb removal when truly needed. Aggressive filters can strip crisp high frequencies and create watery, metallic artifacts. Always A/B listen to the original vs processed clip.
Trim dead air and bad noises: Cut long silent pauses, loud mic bumps, coughs, clicks, and extreme clipping. Keep short, natural pauses between words so phrasing stays human.
Keep clip lengths reasonable: Split very long recordings into clean segments (roughly 3 to 15 seconds each), or let Ilaria RVC's preprocessing slicer segment them cleanly.
Use simple file paths: Store your dataset in a short folder path without spaces, accents, or special symbols (for example C:\RVC\datasets\my_voice\).
Before spending GPU time training, run Ilaria RVC's built-in Dataset Checker to catch hidden audio problems early:
Clipping detection: Finds segments where peaks hit 0 dBFS and flatten out, which can cause harsh distortion or NaN loss during training.
Long silences: Flags clips that are mostly empty air so you can trim or remove them.
Unreadable or broken files: Catches corrupted headers, zero-byte files, or clips shorter than 1 second that would crash preprocessing (zero-size array).
Inconsistent active levels: Highlights clips that are dramatically quieter or louder than the rest of the dataset.
Recommended workflow:
Point the Dataset Checker to your dataset folder and run the scan.
Listen to every flagged file before deleting or editing it.
Preserve natural quiet delivery and intentional pauses when they belong to the voice, and remove or re-clean only genuinely broken, clipped, or noisy clips.
Use the Audio Analyzer to inspect why a recording or conversion sounds wrong:
Waveform peaks: Flat-topped waves indicate hard digital clipping. Lower the gain or replace the clipped recording.

Spectrogram: Look at silent gaps between words. A constant horizontal line at 50/60 Hz points to electrical hum; bright vertical smudges or wash across frequencies indicate leftover music bleed or room reverb.
Pitch & active levels: Check whether the speaker's pitch jumps unnaturally (tracking error) or whether levels drop too low.

Before vs After comparison: Load the exact same region of both the original input and the converted output to tell whether an artifact came from the dataset, the separation step, or inference settings.

l: Change one control at a time
p: Control
A useful first experiment
Pitch shift

Try a small semitone shift if the source lies outside the target voice’s comfortable range. +12 doubles frequency and −12 halves it. Replay a high and a low phrase before applying the change to a song.
Pitch extractor
Compare available estimators when a note jumps or a soft phrase loses voicing. Keep the model, transposition and input fixed.
Search Feature Ratio
With the correct index loaded, increase influence in small steps. Listen for stronger target character, muffled consonants or unwanted source leakage.
Volume Envelope
A value near 0 follows the source dynamics more closely. A value near 1 retains more of the generated dynamics. Compare quiet and loud syllables at a matched playback volume.
Protect Voiceless Consonants
On the current pitch-guided engine, settings below 0.5 activate protection. Lower values increase it. Try a phrase with breaths and consonants such as S, F or T.

Split Audio can help process a long file in pieces. Listen across the joins. Clean Audio can reduce unwanted noise, so compare it against a clean baseline for changes to detail. Proposed Pitch derives a target-directed shift and can interact with manual transposition. Test each by itself. Effects activated through Post-Process apply to the generated audio and can mask a conversion issue.

Speech is present but the target voice sounds weak. Check speaker ID, then compare retrieval only if you have the right index.
The file clips or pulses. Test at a lower source level and turn off processing that changes gain. For singing, compare the isolated vocal before mixing it back into the backing track.

p: Use automatic chunk sizing first where available. If audio breaks up, increase Chunk Size, then repeat exactly the same phrase. Smaller chunks can reduce delay while leaving the engine less time to finish each block. Crossfade Overlap smooths joins, and Extra Conversion Size gives more context at a compute cost. l: Turn a short script into converted speech
p: Applio uses an online Edge TTS voice to read your text and an RVC model to change the generated voice. The source voice determines pronunciation, pacing and the language it reads. Use text you are comfortable sending to the online synthesis service.
Open the text-to-speech workspace after the engine is ready and the voice model works.
Enter one short sentence with punctuation. Choose a source TTS voice for the language of that sentence. Start with its ordinary speaking rate.
Select your RVC inference voice, the matching embedder and its index if you use one. Start with pitch shift at 0 and effects off.

Generate speech and listen to the output. If your interface makes the synthesized source available, play it too. If the source misreads an acronym or pauses oddly, change punctuation, spell out the acronym or select another source voice first.

When the phrase sounds right, save the audio and write down the source voice, speaking rate, RVC model, embedder and pitch. For longer scripts, use small sections with natural breakpoints and keep their settings consistent.

If the speech generation step fails, test a different source voice and check the engine’s connection to the speech service. If speech generation succeeds and only conversion fails, run a short recorded file through the same RVC model. That test exposes model or embedder problems without changing the script.

RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) is the upstream Retrieval-based Voice Conversion WebUI. Use its browser interface for file conversion and training. For microphone conversion, use the separate desktop interface described in the real-time guide.
Your setup
What to use
Windows and a supported GPU
Start with a matching prebuilt Windows archive. This is the shortest route.
Windows and an NVIDIA RTX 50-series GPU
Use a package explicitly marked for the 50 series or the source setup with the CUDA 12.8 Torch build. Older NVIDIA archives can start but fail when they try to run GPU operations.
Windows and an AMD or Intel GPU
Choose the matching AMD/Intel archive. DirectML support depends on the release and operation. Test file conversion first.
Ubuntu or a custom Windows setup
Install the current source branch into a separate Python environment.

Open the RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) Windows package and asset downloads and choose the archive matching your GPU. For the current package family, look for the 20260718 NVIDIA, NVIDIA 50-series, or AMD/Intel variant. If you already have an older release that works, leave it in its own directory.

Extract the entire archive to a writable local folder such as C:\RVC\Mainline. Allow space for both the download and the extracted files. In File Explorer, open the resulting folder and look for the launcher, assets, and the Python runtime. If you see one more enclosing directory, open it.

Run go-webui.bat if present. Older archives may call it go-web.bat. Keep the command window open and wait for the local address. If the browser does not start, open the address shown in the terminal. A common default is http://127.0.0.1:7865.
Confirm that the page opens and that the terminal remains running. Keep the archive intact until the first conversion succeeds.

Recommended on Windows: download the ready-to-use Windows archive for your GPU. Installing from source is discouraged for most users because you have to configure Python and its dependencies yourself.

Download and extract the RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) source ZIP. Open a terminal in the directory containing webui.py and the requirements files. The source setup below applies to the Python 3.12 branch. Run each snippet from that directory using a 64-bit Python 3.12 interpreter.

l: Convert recordings in RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC)
p: Start with a short recording that you can hear clearly in a normal media player, plus an exported RVC model you have permission to use. The model changes the voice in the recording. The source provides the words, rhythm and delivery. For a song, use a separately recorded or isolated vocal track for the first pass.

l: Put each file in the right place
p: What you received
Where it goes
A ZIP or 7z with a model inside
Extract the files before adding them to RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC).
An inference .pth file
Copy it to assets/weights/ inside the RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) folder. If you trained it yourself, use the exported small model.
A populated .index for that exact model
In current builds, copy it to assets/indices/. Older builds commonly discover indexes under logs/. If auto-detection fails, select it or enter its full path manually.
A G_*.pth or D_*.pth training checkpoint
Keep it with the experiment in logs/. Use the training guide to identify or export a model for inference.

Use added_*.index when training produced both trained_ and added_ files. The latter contains the searchable feature vectors. Your model can work with no index. Set Index Rate to zero when you skip the index or cannot identify its matching file.

Open the WebUI and find the Model Inference tab. Refresh the model and index lists after copying files, then select the inference .pth in the voice dropdown. Give the interface time to read the checkpoint.

Choose a short WAV with one voice speaking or singing on its own. Newer builds expose an upload control. If your build shows a path box, give it a full path such as C:\RVC\test\voice.wav. Try a short local path when diagnosing file access in an older package.

Set pitch shift to 0 for the first pass. Set Index Rate or Search feature ratio to 0, and leave extra settings as they are. Select rmvpe if available and its weights are installed. With a single-speaker checkpoint, start with speaker ID 0.

Click Convert once and wait for the status and playback panel. Play the result from the beginning. If it sounds usable, use the audio player's menu to download it. If conversion fails, read the status or terminal before changing settings.
Replay the same source and output back to back. Check the first word, the highest and lowest notes, and several pauses. Change one control and rerender the same input to tell which change helped.

l: Understand the controls you are likely to touch
p: Changes how closely the result follows loud and quiet moments in the input. Closer to zero follows the source more.
Control

Controls how much the conversion preserves unvoiced detail, such as breaths and consonants. Lower values strengthen protection in the usual RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) 0–0.5 control. Try a small adjustment after index retrieval works.
Estimates the pitch contour used in pitch-guided conversion. Try another method when voice breaks appear on certain notes. Compare the same clip and keep everything else constant.
How to use it
Index Rate
Mixes in nearby features from the target voice when a matching index exists. Increase it gradually if the result keeps too much of the source timbre. Back it down if diction gets muddy.
Pitch extraction
Pitch shift
Protect
Resample output
Selects a voice within a multi-speaker checkpoint. Choose an ID actually present in that model.
Sets the exported audio sample rate where the build exposes it. Leave it at the model default during your first test.
Speaker ID
Transposes the source in semitones. +12 raises it an octave, -12 lowers it an octave. Make small moves first when words or notes sound strained.
Volume envelope

Save an unprocessed 10-second source as test.wav. Convert it with zero pitch shift and no index to get baseline.wav. Load the matching index and raise its rate for retrieval.wav. Compare those two files at similar volume. Once you choose a retrieval setting, try a pitch adjustment and save a third file. Keep whichever setting improves the same troublesome line without degrading the rest.
Finish a successful single-file test using the same voice and settings.
Create separate input and output folders. Put only the audio you want converted in input.
Under Batch Inference, choose your files or enter the full input-folder path. Set the output-folder path explicitly and choose WAV if you plan to edit the audio later.

l: Train and export a RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) model
p: Start with a single speaker and a fresh experiment name. Training produces a model you can test on new performances in the inference interface. Keep raw audio and the experiment log so you can reproduce your result.

Put clean voice recordings in a local folder such as C:\RVC\datasets\voice_a. Keep backups elsewhere. Use recordings you have permission to train with. Check that you can play several files and that they contain the intended voice without backing music or unrelated speakers.

Keep one or two short recordings of different phrases outside the dataset. Use these as test inputs for every checkpoint. For a dataset intended for singing, make sure you have material with the relevant vocal range and test with an isolated vocal.
If you installed from source, open the same environment used to run the WebUI and get the matching pretrained weights and silence assets. Packaged releases may already contain them.
See dataset preparation for recording and cleanup details.

l: Configure the experiment and process audio
p: Open Train. Use a fresh name such as voice_a_v2_40k so RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) creates a separate folder under logs/.

Choose a target sample rate and architecture version supported by your release. V2 is a reasonable starting point when you plan to use a compatible V2 inference client. Rate, architecture, and pitch guidance must agree with the generator and discriminator pretrains. Use pitch guidance for a normal pitch-guided voice model.

Select a single-speaker dataset, where the build offers a choice. Use speaker ID 0 for the first run. Paste the complete dataset folder path, then click Process Data or the equivalent preprocessing button.

Wait for preprocessing to finish. Review warnings in the output and check that the experiment has produced processed audio. If the run produces nothing, verify the path and test whether the included audio files decode. Fix this before starting extraction.

For a multi-speaker experiment on a build with Multi-speaker Dataset Helper, keep each speaker's files separate and assign stable speaker IDs. Check the generated manifest and use those same IDs later during conversion. Complete a single-speaker pass first so you have a working baseline.
Choose the GPU index shown by the interface. For one GPU the ID is commonly 0. Device fields for different operations may be separate. Copy the available IDs instead of assuming a specific slot.

Select a pitch extractor that the build can run. If a GPU RMVPE option is available and works on your system, start there. A CPU option can help isolate a backend problem. Feature extraction also requires the shared HuBERT assets installed in setup.

Run Feature extraction and wait for both the required pitch and the content-feature stages to finish. If a stage logs no usable files, stop and correct the cause. Changing the dataset, model version, or target rate changes the experiment. Use a new experiment name when comparing incompatible settings.

Generic HuBERT checkpoints are not recommended as the default encoder for voice conversion. Their speech prediction training does not explicitly remove speaker identity, so the features can carry source timbre into the output. For RVC, use the encoder expected by the model, such as ContentVec when the voice was trained with it.

Check the generator and discriminator fields in the training panel. They should refer to a matched pair for the version, sample rate and pitch mode you selected. If a log says the files were skipped, make sure you are training with the intended setup before continuing.

Start with a batch that fits memory and leave dataset caching off for the first test. If the GPU runs out of memory, stop the failed job and lower the batch size. Avoid running a live conversion alongside the first training run.

Set a finite trial target and an interval that saves multiple checkpoints you can compare later. If you want intermediate models ready for inference, enable small model exports at save time where available. Keeping only the latest training checkpoints saves space but limits resuming from earlier versions.

Click Train model. Watch the experiment status and confirm the training log advances across epochs. Use the application's stop control when available and wait for it to finish writing files before closing the process.

Training curves reveal whether the job is running or producing errors. Choose the final model by converting the same test recordings with several saved inference exports. Compare words, consonants, pauses and difficult notes at similar volume. More epochs can help, plateau or make results worse depending on the dataset.
Back up the small inference model and its matching index to use or share. Keep the experiment folder, including matching G_*.pth and D_*.pth, configuration and logs, if you plan to resume training.
Check the dataset path, permissions, supported formats and whether the WAV files open outside RVC.

Click Train feature index after successful extraction if you want a retrieval index. Look for the populated added_*.index in the experiment output, with a discoverable copy or link if provided by your build. Skip retrieval if you only want to evaluate the checkpoint itself.
Confirm you selected an exported inference model. Test a known working checkpoint with the same input and no index.
Convert a held-out clip at zero index rate. Once that works, try the matching populated index. Save both outputs for comparison.
Feature extraction stops

Find the small exported model under assets/weights/. If you have only a generator checkpoint, use ckpt Processing and the small model extraction tool, supplying the matching rate, pitch flag and version. Refresh the model list in inference and select the small export.
Identify whether content or pitch extraction failed. Check model assets and try a supported backend.
Index generation finds no features
Inference fails with a checkpoint
Preprocessing finishes with no audio
Reduce batch size, switch off caching and free VRAM before retrying.
Revisit successful feature extraction for the same experiment. Check version and folder names before trying to reuse files.

In a Windows package with go-realtime_gui.bat, launch it from the unpacked program folder. In the current source branch, activate the environment from setup and run python realtime_gui.py from the repository directory. Package launcher names vary.

In the real-time window, select the small inference .pth. If you have its matching populated .index, choose it here. Leave Index Rate at 0 for the first listening test. If your build requires an index in its file picker, supply the one for the selected model.

Choose a sound host interface, then select your physical microphone as input and headphones as output. Choose the normal values for pitch and sample rate offered by your build. Start with default performance settings.

l: Verify the microphone before connecting an app
p: Lower the headphone volume before starting. If the GUI offers Input voice monitor, use it to confirm the selected microphone. Speak a short sentence and pause. Check that you hear one direct voice and silence during the pause.

Switch to Output converted voice and start conversion. Wait for initialization. Repeat the same sentence at an ordinary speaking level and listen to consonants and word endings. Check for feedback before raising the volume.

If the stream starts but clips words, check the device selection and input level. If there are repeated gaps, return to the default processing block length. A clean, slightly delayed voice is a better baseline than a low-latency signal that keeps breaking up.
Stop the stream before changing audio devices or loading a different checkpoint. Restart and repeat the same listening test.

l: Route RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) into a call or recorder
p: Set up a virtual cable or other pair of connected playback and recording devices. The playback end receives sound from RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC). The recording end supplies that sound to your call or recorder.

In the destination app, choose the cable's recording end as its microphone. Select your headphones for that app's playback so sound from the call does not travel back through the cable.

Start conversion and make a private recording or use the app's microphone test. Confirm that it captures the converted voice once. If you also need local monitoring, use the destination app's monitoring where available and keep it separate from the cable input.
If the destination app cuts quiet syllables, compare a short sample with automatic noise processing off for diagnosis. Restore any processing that improves the result without losing words.

Confirm you chose the two ends of the same cable. Test both endpoints with a local recording app.

Decrease Sample length or the equivalent block control one increment at a time. A shorter block reduces waiting but gives the engine less time to finish. Repeat a quiet phrase and a louder phrase after each change. If there are clicks, dropouts or repeated syllables, go back to the last stable value. Once the block size is stable, adjust one other setting at a time if your build exposes it:
Device is missing
Extra inference time gives the model more context around the current block. Reduce it cautiously and listen for instability.
Fade length blends overlapping chunks. A change can help with clicks at chunk boundaries.
Good monitor sound, silent destination
Howl or doubled voice
Index rate and noise reductions add processing. Try a stable baseline with the optional features off before tuning each one.
Model will not start
Pitch extraction affects both pitch quality and workload. Compare a supported alternative when difficult notes wobble or processing takes too long.
See real-time conversion basics for other supported apps and general routing terminology.
Set the downstream microphone to the cable's recording end. Disable a second capture source if the app mixes both.
Stop the stream, reload the device list, and try another host interface that exposes the microphone and output. Check system microphone permission.

Test the same inference export in the WebUI and confirm the matching assets. Check the first GUI error before changing device and model settings together.
The downstream app receives the raw voice
Use headphones, check that no input points to the cable's own return, and switch off duplicate monitoring.

p: Plug in your microphone and headphones before opening VCClient. In the operating system, speak into the microphone and check that the input meter moves. Pause Discord, OBS and other capture apps during this test.

In Model Selection, choose a compatible sample model if one is available. For your own model, use Edit, pick a spare slot and choose Upload. Select RVC when the dialog requests a model type. p: Client uses devices available to the client/browser. Microphone permissions and the browser's output selection can affect the device list. On one PC, test the simpler client path first. Switch to Server if your build exposes a separate monitor or the browser cannot select the desired output endpoint. In Server mode, choose the host API and device names offered by the server. If several entries share a name, try using the same audio API for input and output. Once the signal is stable, you can test alternatives for latency.

Set VCClient input to the physical microphone. Set the converter's output to the cable's playback endpoint. With VB-CABLE, this is commonly CABLE Input.

Select the cable's recording endpoint as the target microphone. With VB-CABLE, that is commonly CABLE Output. In OBS, select that device for the audio input capture and mute any second capture of the physical mic.

Use a test call or make a short local recording in the target app. Test quiet and loud speech. Confirm that stopping VCClient or muting the converted source makes its meter stop. If it continues, the target has another input active or is receiving an unintended route.

Compare destination noise suppression or automatic gain on and off only if the converter sounds good locally and the target chops syllables or changes the level. Keep the options that work for your room and microphone.

Choose a pitch estimator that handles your normal speaking range. Compare the same phrase at each setting. Hold the model and microphone gain steady during the comparison.

If words cut out, increase it again or reduce extra context. Crossfade helps soften boundaries but also consumes part of the available processing budget.

l: 2. Load a model and tune settings
p: Upload or select an inference RVC .pth model and its optional matching .index file.

Chunk / Block size: start around 0.3s to 0.5s (or 192 / 256+ samples/frames depending on the UI slider) to balance delay and audio smoothness. Lowering Chunk too far causes robotic stutter or dropouts.
Extra Data / Context: keep moderate (0.5s to 1.0s) for stable tone without overloading the GPU.
F0 / Pitch detector: use RMVPE (most accurate) or FCPE (lighter/faster for real-time); avoid heavy Crepe Full in live mode if inference time exceeds chunk time.
Tune (Pitch): +12 for male to female, -12 for female to male, 0 for same range.
Index ratio: start at 0.0 to test clean conversion, then raise gently (0.3 to 0.6) if needed.
High latency or robotic stutter: disable Hardware-accelerated GPU Scheduling (HAGS) in Windows Graphics Settings and restart, close GPU-heavy games/browser tabs, and raise Chunk one step.
PortAudio / device error: match all audio devices to the same sample rate (48000 Hz) in Windows Sound settings and close apps holding exclusive device control.

This guide covers Tiger14n's archived desktop app for converting audio files. Prepare a voice checkpoint and a short, dry WAV recording before you start.
Open the project's Windows package. Download the packaged asset from the release, and extract the contents to a writable folder. Keep the runtime and model assets in the extracted layout.

Open the included launcher. A source checkout can be started with RVC-GUI.bat on Windows or python rvcgui.py once the runtime is set up. The archived source expects a compatible Python and PyTorch environment plus hubert_base.pt in its project root. Use a separate environment if you are testing the source so other RVC installations retain their dependencies.

If the packaged app closes immediately, run its launcher from an open terminal and read the first error. An archive that contains source files only will not have the packaged runtime. If the error names HuBERT in a source install, place the project's HuBERT weights in the project root.

Generic HuBERT checkpoints are not recommended as the default encoder for voice conversion. Their speech prediction training does not explicitly remove speaker identity, so the features can carry source timbre into the output. For RVC, use the encoder expected by the model, such as ContentVec when the voice was trained with it.

Click Import model from .zip and select a ZIP containing an inference .pth and its matching .index if supplied. For manual placement, put the files in a per-voice subfolder under the app's models directory. For example:

Select the imported voice in the GUI. If it is absent, reopen the model list or restart the app after checking the folder. Use an inference model compatible with the archived build. A model created with an encoder or architecture the build cannot load should be tested in a compatible app.

Important notes before you start
This tool is strictly a model merger: it does not convert audio, run live microphone conversion, or train new models. It only blends two or more existing RVC .pth models into a new .pth file.

Cross-sample-rate merging is supported: despite what the repository README states, you can merge models with different sample rates (e.g. 32k, 40k, 48k) using Encoder-only merge, as long as they share the same RVC version (v1 or v2) and same vocoder architecture (HiFi-GAN or RefineGAN).

YuneVoix is a real-time AI voice conversion application for Windows, powered by the YUNE engine. Just like RVC, it transforms your voice into someone else's - for both speech and singing, live or offline - but without training a voice model. Everything runs locally on your own graphics card: no cloud, no account, and your audio never leaves your PC.

Instead of spending hours training a model on a dataset, YUNE only needs a short reference audio sample of the target voice (about 5–20 seconds). It splits your voice into what you say and how you say it:
Speech encoder: captures your words, articulation, and timing.
Pitch tracker: follows your melody and intonation.
Diffusion-transformer model: rebuilds the audio in the target voice's timbre using the short reference recording.
Neural vocoder: outputs full-band 44.1 kHz audio.
In LIVE mode, audio is processed in small blocks of about 160 ms, with roughly 0.7 seconds of total end-to-end delay at default settings.

Causal Voice Changer (CVC) is a 48 kHz real-time AI voice changer built to bridge the gap between ultra-low-latency systems (like Beatrice) and slower, high-fidelity systems (like RVC). Instead of trading away sound quality for speed - or speed for quality - CVC uses a distilled version of ContentVec and RMVPE in a causal architecture to deliver both clean audio and low delay.

l: How CVC differs from RVC (explained simply)
p: Traditional RVC was originally designed to convert complete audio files, not live streams:
RVC grabs a block of your voice, converts it, and stitches it onto the previous block using a crossfade.

When you lower the block size to reduce delay, RVC has less context - so quality and pitch accuracy drop. If you hold a note or draw out a word, you can often hear the seams between blocks as warbling or crackling.
Causal Voice Changer (CVC) works differently:
It is causal: it converts audio continuously as it arrives, looking mostly backward with only a 60 ms lookahead buffer.
Because it streams continuously instead of stitching independent chunks, sustained sounds and held notes stay smooth without breaking or warbling.
You keep nearly all the quality of RVC at a much lower latency (for example, around 130 ms total end-to-end on Linux with JACK audio).
While CVC's source code is under the MIT license, the included pretrained base model was trained on EARS (CC BY-NC), VCTK, and LibriTTS-R.
Non-commercial use only: Because of the EARS dataset, you may not use the included pretrained base model - or any voice finetuned from it - for commercial purposes.

Input → Source:
Choose Microphone / audio device for live speech.
(Or choose Audio file to test a voice by playing a pre-recorded file through the model.)
Input device: select your physical microphone.
Output device: select where the converted voice should go.
To use CVC in Discord, OBS, VRChat, or games, install a virtual audio cable (such as VB-CABLE on Windows) and choose CABLE Input here, then pick CABLE Output as your microphone in Discord/OBS.
Monitor device (optional): select your headphones if you want to hear your own converted voice. Leave Disabled if you don't want to hear yourself.
(Linux tip): [JACK] devices give the lowest latency. You can set the PipeWire period with PIPEWIRE_QUANTUM, e.g. 128/48000.
Pick your Model (and Checkpoint if the voice has multiple saved steps).
Pitch (semitones): shift your voice up or down to match the target voice (+12 = one octave up, -12 = one octave down).
Pitch match: don't guess! Drop clips of the model's voice into Pitch match to measure its median Hz, then talk while converting so CVC measures your voice and suggests the exact shift (Apply).
Advanced pitch (collapsed by default - most voices don't need it):
Pitch offset (Hz): adds a fixed Hz offset after the semitone shift. Positive values raise low notes more than high notes (narrowing range); negative values widen it.
Pitch ceiling (Hz) & Above the ceiling (%): pulls down squeaky high peaks above the ceiling while keeping notes below it in tune (great for singing; 0% stops strictly at the ceiling).
Formant: shifts vocal resonance (how "big" or "small" the speaker sounds) without changing pitch (0 = model's natural formant).
Index (%) (off by default): blends each 20 ms of speech toward the closest moments in the voice's training audio. Higher sounds closer to the target speaker, but too high can blur words.
Consonant protection (only applies when Index > 0): keeps breaths and consonants (s, t, k) closer to your own so words stay crisp.
Input gain: boosts or cuts your microphone before conversion.
Output gain: controls the volume sent to Discord/OBS/games.
Monitor gain: controls only what you hear in your headphones.
Noise gate: mutes your mic when you're quieter than the threshold (-60 dB = off).
Output level (LUFS): talk while converting to see your loudness and click Apply to auto-adjust Output gain toward Voice chat (-21 LUFS) or Streaming (-16 LUFS).
Click Start to begin live conversion, or Passthrough to send your raw mic straight through for quick volume checks.
Watch In / Out / Mon meters and the two timing readouts:
Latency: total delay from mic to output.
Inference: time your GPU takes to convert one chunk. Inference must stay well below your Chunk size (e.g., 10 ms for a 20 ms chunk), otherwise the audio will stutter.
You can record your sessions directly inside CausalVC Realtime (start conversion first):
Chunk (steps of 20 ms): how much audio is converted at a time. Total delay is CVC's fixed 60 ms lookahead + 1 chunk + your sound card/virtual cable buffers.
Lower chunks = lower latency, but require a faster GPU.
If audio crackles or stutters (or if you are running on CPU on an older AMD card), raise Chunk to 40 ms or 60 ms+.
Extra inference buffer: how much recent speech the model looks back at for each chunk. More context gives steadier tone and pitch at a small GPU cost, with zero added delay.
Pitch detector:
RMVPE (recommended): most accurate.
FCPE: lighter on the GPU.
PM (fastest): fastest, but roughest.
Pitch smoothing (RMVPE only): tracks pitch as one continuous line so held notes don't wobble or flip octaves (no added delay).
Volume envelope: 0 matches your microphone's loudness moment-to-moment; 1 keeps the model's own loudness.

Fast GPU replay (on by default): records the GPU's work once and replays it for every chunk - roughly 2× faster and much steadier (for example, an RTX 5050 converts a 20 ms chunk in 4.4 ms instead of 9.7 ms). Turn it off only if your GPU converts wrongly or fails to start with it.
Audio seam & quality helpers:
Soften sudden treble: smooths brief clicks when treble switches on mid-word (adds 5 ms delay).
Match level across seams: keeps high-frequency levels steady between chunks (no added delay).
Hold context during silence: remembers your last words during pauses so the first word after silence isn't slurred.
Silence detection: Loudness (-50 dBFS) is best for quiet rooms; Voice detection (experimental) uses RNNoise so fans/hum don't count as speech.
Input noise reduction: removes keyboard, fan, or room noise before conversion:
Hushwire (Amazon Voice Focus) (default): strongest cleanup and most natural voice; adds about 55 ms delay. Its model is downloaded once from Amazon's servers only after you accept the prompt.
RNNoise: lighter cleanup with lower delay (20 ms).
Output noise reduction: cleans hiss from the converted voice using spectral gating. Leave off unless you hear hiss, as it can make the voice slightly duller.

UVR5 (Ultimate Vocal Remover v5 GUI) is a free, open-source desktop application for AI audio source separation. It runs locally on your PC and lets you split songs or dialogue into clean vocals, instrumentals, backing vocals, individual stems (drums, bass, other), and remove reverb, echo, and background noise - making it one of the most popular tools for preparing RVC datasets and covers.
VR Architecture (v4, v5, v5.1): fast, reliable models great for vocals, karaoke (lead vs. backing), de-echo, de-reverb, and denoising.
MDX-Net (v2, MDX23C, plus BS-Roformer, Mel-Roformer, SCNet, and Bandit in beta Roformer patches): state-of-the-art architectures grouped under the MDX-Net menu in UVR5.
Demucs (v1–v4, such as htdemucs and htdemucs_ft): Meta's multi-stem models (4 stems: vocals, drums, bass, other; or 6 stems) ideal for isolating instruments or building ensembles.
Built-in Audio Tools: Manual Ensemble (combine outputs from multiple models via Min/Max Spec or Average), Ensemble Mode, Vocal Splitter, Demudder (Windows patch #14+), and Apollo audio upscaler.
Platform
Requirements & Acceleration Notes
Windows 10/11 (64-bit)
Must be installed on the C:\ drive (secondary drives can cause instability). Intel Pentium and Celeron CPUs are not guaranteed to work.

Maxwell (GTX 900 series, compute 5.0) or newer. GTX 600 / GT 700 and older are unsupported for CUDA. 6 GB+ VRAM (e.g. RTX 3050 6–8 GB or better) is recommended for Roformers; 2–4 GB works with smaller chunk_size / dim_t values. RTX 5000 series requires the dedicated CUDA 12.8 patch.

Uses DirectML (labeled OpenCL in older v5.6.0 builds). Tested on AMD RX 4 GB+ (RX 6600 XT / 7600+ recommended for Roformers) and Intel Arc / Xe iGPUs. 16 GB VRAM is recommended if using default Roformer chunk_size (otherwise lower chunk_size). Note: Apollo, Bandit, and SCNet fall back to CPU on DirectML.
macOS
macOS Big Sur or newer (Catalina or lower not guaranteed). Apple Silicon (MPS) acceleration works for Demucs, MDX-Net, and Roformers. Place UVR directly inside root /Applications.

Native v5.6.0_roformer_add+directml branch, or run the Windows installer inside Bottles (WINE gaming profile in drive_c) for newer Roformer patches with GPU acceleration.

p: Download Ilaria RVC 2.4.0 for Windows (ZIP)

Voice conversion starts with a performance. The output usually follows the source words, timing, articulation, and pitch contour while changing the sound of the voice. Decisions about delivery still start with the original recording. For a sung cover, plan to convert an isolated lead vocal and mix the converted vocal with the instrumental afterward.

Open Ilaria RVC and import the inference model you want to use. An optional index belongs with the checkpoint it was built for. If an imported voice is absent from the selector, see RVC models and files.
Open Single Inference, choose the voice, and drag in a short recording you can recognize by ear. A phrase with a pause, several consonants, and a longer vowel makes a useful reference.

Set Pitch to zero and Index Ratio to zero. Match the content embedder to the one used in training when the model author provides it. Start with the app's default pitch extractor and leave optional audio processing off.
Convert the file and check the output. Use the waveform player to revisit the same phrase, then save a WAV or FLAC copy as your baseline.
Compare the original and the converted clip at similar playback levels. Note the first audible problem and use Pitch and audio quality to decide what to change.

Current Ilaria RVC releases automatically look for a matching index when you select a voice. Selecting an index and giving it influence are separate actions. A loaded index contributes only when Index Ratio is above zero. Older builds may show a different layout or ask you to select the index manually.

l: Choose a source that fits the job
p: A consistent voice across takes recorded at different levels or pitches.
A lead vocal over music
Clear words, intact word endings, and consistent tone between phrases.
Correct pronunciation and intentional pacing before the RVC stage.
Dialogue or narration

If a separated vocal still contains loud cymbals or another singer, compare it with a cleaner take or separation. Those sounds reach the conversion engine along with the intended voice. Keep breaths and word endings where they matter to the performance.
Isolate the lead. Leave the instrumental, backing voices, and harmonies on their own tracks.
Label each take by scene or section and keep the original file names in your notes.
Listen for
Multiple takes
Prepare the source
Preview the generated speech before applying the model. Adjust punctuation or phrasing in the text first.
Spoken text through TTS
Stable sustained notes and consonants that still line up with the beat.
Use one speaker per input track and keep a short natural pause between lines.
Workflow

Open Batch Inference after a single file produces a usable result. Group files that need the same model, pitch, and processing profile. Run one representative file from each group and save to a separate output location so you can compare results safely.

For a long song, audition a section with exposed high or low notes before converting the whole file. Split Audio can help with long recordings or memory limitations. Listen across segment joins and pauses after the run. If a version of the app exposes a console or conversion log, use it to identify any failed items and retry those files separately.

In a release with the TTS workspace, supply text or a UTF-8 text file. Current Ilaria RVC releases offer Microsoft Edge online voices and installed Windows voices for offline TTS. Pick a source voice in the language of the script, listen for pronunciation and pauses, and then apply the RVC model to that generated recording. If the first stage reads a name incorrectly, fix the text or change the TTS voice first. RVC will generally carry those source pronunciation choices through.
When privacy or an unreliable connection matters, select an installed Windows voice and check that it works with your text before starting a long job. The Edge option requires a network connection.

l: Save the conversion and your settings
p: Keep an unprocessed WAV or FLAC master before adding compression, reverb, or limiting.
For music, align the converted vocal against the original, check its timing at consonants, and listen to both solo and in the mix before exporting.

Save your settings alongside the result. Include the source file, model and index versions, speaker ID if applicable, embedder, pitch extractor, pitch shift, index ratio, processing, and output format.
When a model is missing or inference fails before producing audio, start with Troubleshooting. For microphone conversion, see Real-time voice conversion.

l: Convert a recording in RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC)

p: On Windows, use a RVC WebUI (Mainline - Original RVC) package compatible with your hardware. Extract the entire archive to a local directory before running its launcher. Windows packages that include go-web.bat use it to start the local WebUI. Leave the console open while converting. If the browser does not open automatically, use the local address printed in the console.

Place the inference checkpoint in assets/weights and its matching retrieval index, if supplied, under logs. Open Model Inference and refresh the voice and index lists. Choose the checkpoint and matching index. Set the retrieval ratio to zero for models without an index.

Give the WebUI the full path to a short local WAV file. If the path fails, copy the test file to a simple location such as C:\RVC\input\test.wav. Keep transposition at zero for the first pass and select RMVPE if your build offers it. Click Convert, then listen in the output player and save the result using its download control. If generation fails, read the console message before changing settings. A model that does not appear in the list usually needs to be moved to the weights directory or rediscovered using refresh.

In Desktop, wait until the engine is ready, add the inference model to the library, and open Convert Audio in single-file mode. In Gradio, open the browser interface and select Convert Audio or Inference, depending on the release. Refresh the model list after adding a checkpoint if it is missing.

Select the voice and its paired index, then confirm the content embedder expected by that model. Load a short recording and choose WAV or FLAC for the test. Check for settings carried over from a previous run, especially pitch, retrieval and effects. A useful baseline starts at zero semitones with effects off. Start the job once, wait for the output, and compare the same phrase in both recordings.

p: What you hear
What to try
Notes jump or wobble
Compare pitch extractors using the same phrase, then test transposition separately.

Pick a short excerpt that contains the problem. Make a reference conversion and compare it with one changed setting at a time. Listen at similar levels so a louder result does not win the comparison by volume alone. For music, compare the converted vocal alone first and then in the mix.

Pitch measures how high or low a voiced sound is. F0, or fundamental frequency, is the periodic part of the signal from which a pitch extractor estimates the contour. A pitch-guided model uses that contour when it synthesizes the output.

Pitch shifts that contour by semitones. Positive values raise it and negative values lower it. Each octave has 12 semitones. For example, applying +12 to a voiced note at 220 Hz gives 440 Hz. A setting of zero keeps the pitch reference from the recording.

For speech, start at zero. If the clip sits far outside the target model's comfortable range or sounds strained, compare with a small shift up or down. For singing over an existing instrumental, compare zero first. A shift that changes the key of the vocal can clash with the backing track. Octave shifts keep the note names, though the model still needs to handle the resulting range. Compare the lowest and highest exposed notes before committing to a whole song.

Formants describe resonances that help distinguish vowels and voice character. Use formant processing only after the pitch contour is working. Pitch and resonance can need different adjustments. In builds with both inference pitch and a pitch-shift effect, the former changes the extracted pitch before synthesis and the latter acts on the resulting audio.

Start with RMVPE, the default for current Ilaria RVC inference. If the pitch is unstable, test another extractor available in your build, such as FCPE or Swift. Keep the same input, pitch shift, index ratio and output format for each run.
For a held note, listen for sudden doubling or halving of the pitch. If several extractors fail at the same timestamp, check for another singer, an instrument in the vocal stem, or severe clipping.
For quiet speech, make sure the input contains a clear voiced vowel. Increasing the level of a clip that contains mostly noise can make it harder to diagnose.
For a large batch, compare an excerpt from the lowest and highest source voices first. Benchmark processing time with the same file and settings on the intended machine.
Pitch extraction and content extraction are separate stages. Changing the F0 extractor estimates a different pitch contour from the same audio. The content embedder still needs to match the model.

What to collect

Questions, statements, longer sentences, and short responses with varied consonants and vowels.

The intended delivery styles at both quiet and emphatic levels. Record variations across several phrases.

ContentVec can be a bottleneck in multilingual models. A dataset containing the target language cannot guarantee that the encoder preserves its phonetic distinctions. Set aside recordings for each language, including difficult sound contrasts, and compare pronunciation after a short training run. If the same errors recur on clean test clips, document the limitation for that language. Changing the encoder or training configuration does not reliably resolve it.

A clean, varied set of recordings is a better starting point than a larger collection of repeated phrases or damaged audio. There is no duration that guarantees a good result. Audit what the recordings cover before deciding whether you need more material.

20 minutes

A recording can be free of noise and still cover very little of a voice. Build the session around the performance you expect to convert. For narration, record clear reading with intentional phrasing. For conversation, include spontaneous replies and changes in pace. For singing, collect dry a cappella takes across the intended register, with sustained vowels and transitions between notes. What to capture

Capture a single microphone on a mono track. Use a pop filter or windscreen, keep the mic distance consistent, and set gain while testing the loudest planned line. A quiet room with soft furnishings reduces reflections at the source. Prefer a dry original over a heavily cleaned recording with audible reverb or separation artifacts. If converting existing stereo recordings to mono, listen to both channels and the fold-down. Use a clean channel if the combined signal sounds hollow or loses detail.

Sample rate: Keep the originals at their recorded rate. Choose a training rate supported by the architecture and pretrained weights. The preprocessing stage can resample when needed. Upsampling adds no detail to the original recording.

Levels: Compare session levels and fix large gain differences caused by mic placement or recording settings. Preserve intentional changes in delivery. Check what the training frontend already normalizes before applying a separate loudness pass.
Breaths and reactions: Keep natural breaths and clean expressive cues where they serve the intended use. Trim clipped laughs, harsh gasps, and plosive bursts. Audition uncertain edits in headphones.

Pauses: Keep natural pauses and remove long empty spans. If you want to test a standalone silence clip, run a comparison with the same settings and listen to held-out pauses. Some preprocessing pipelines already handle silence.
Use one speaker for a first model. Exclude overlapping voices, crowd responses, and dialogue where the speaker changes mid-clip.
Listen for fan noise, echoes, music, and digital distortion. A clip that sounds acceptable in a loud mix can still contain problems that are obvious when the voice is isolated.
If you are recording a new session, use a consistent mic position and leave peak headroom. Test the loudest phrase before recording the full session.
When combining sessions, listen to them side by side. Keep useful variation in the voice and discard abrupt differences caused by heavy effects, room sound, or an unreliable microphone.
Remove duplicate takes if they add little variety. Put different sessions or passages aside for evaluation before editing adjacent cuts into the training folder.

Isolate the target voice. If the source includes an accompaniment, try separation and audition the resulting vocal stem. Reject sections with instrument bleed, backing vocals, or obvious separation artifacts.
Make cuts at natural boundaries. Trim long dead air and remove unusable sections. Listen across each cut for lost consonants, abrupt changes, or a second speaker entering.

Apply only the cleanup the recording needs. Compare any denoising pass against the original. If the cleaned version swallows consonants, blurs syllables, or introduces a pulsing sound, reduce the processing or replace the take.

Check levels across files. Keep enough headroom for loud passages and balance major recording-level differences. Lowering the volume of an already clipped file leaves the damaged peaks in the recording.
Export in a lossless format your build can read. WAV is a practical working format. Re-encoding a compressed file as WAV preserves the result of that decode and cannot restore lost detail.

The training engine may divide files into its own segments and resample them to the selected model configuration. Keep usable words and phrases intact during manual editing and let the training preprocessing stage handle its own segmentation.
